items.action: The generic term 'barca' was long used for any small river-traffic or fishing boat on the Tagus.
Records list many river boats (barcas and batéis) serving Lisbon, while ships from across Christendom entered the port each year and anchored offshore.

numbers.what: naus and other ships entering Lisbon port annually

items.action: Anchored ships offshore were supplied by various types of small boats.
From the early 16th century barcas began to diversify according to their functions and the routes they sailed on the Tagus.
Going upriver, entering shallow creeks, carrying varied cargo and fishing in river and sea required boats with differing keels, flat bottoms, bows, masts and sails.
River traffic linked the two banks, coast and interior, and mouth and Riba-Tejo, carrying goods and people and supporting fishing, until the mid-20th century.
Fishermen, sailors, shipwrights and caulkers built traditional wooden boats in shipyards concentrated in riverside towns.
Larger shipyards stood on the south bank, while smaller artisanal yards existed at other named places.
items.place: Aldeagalega (Montijo), Alcochete, Sarilhos Pequenos, Barreiro, Seixal, Amora, Ar

items.action: Upstream shipyards are also recorded at Valada, Punhete (Constância) and Rossio ao Sul do Tejo.
items.place: Valada, Punhete (Constância), Rossio ao Sul do Tejo

items.action: Boat shapes, sizes and colours varied with function, route navigability and the style of each yard or town.
Well-known passenger boats included catraio, caíque, bote, batel, canoa, falua and bote cacilheiro.
items.boat: catraio, caíque, bote, batel, canoa, falua, bote cacilheiro

items.action: Well-known cargo boats included mill boats, Riba-Tejo boats, cargueiros, bateiras, faluas, canoa cacilheira, varinos and fragatas.
items.boat: barcos dos moinhos, barcos de Riba-Tejo, cargueiros, bateira

items.action: Fishing boats named are caíques, saveiros and muletas; varinos and fragatas were the most representative cargo vessels of the Tagus.
The varino was an elegant, decorated boat resembling a large two-ended bateira, with a pronounced toothed bow and a lateen sail on a backward-leaning mast.
The varino had a bulging keelless hull, two decks with bulkheads, and a hold with paneiros and false bulwarks for stowing cargo.
The fragata was a solid, open-mouthed, flat-sterned boat with one backward-leaning mast, a large gaff sail and one or two headsails, no oars, fixed rudder.
items.gear: vela de carangueja, velas de proa

items.action: Fragatas loaded and unloaded ships anchored in Lisbon harbour and handled cargo at quays on both banks.
items.place: porto de Lisboa, cais de ambas as margens

items.action: Fragatas varied in size, with a keeled hull and two cabins, one forward and one aft.
A fragata had a small crew and, without favourable wind, was rowed along by a small boat usually towed behind it.
The term fragata was also applied generally to similar Tagus boats, such as faluas, a medium size between bote and large fragata.
Paddle-wheel and later propeller steamers began carrying passengers between the river's two banks, gradually displacing the small boats that had done the same job.
items.boat: vapores (steamers) with paddle wheels, then propellers

items.action: The Vila Franca de Xira bridge opened, speeding goods transport between the banks; upriver river navigation lost impact and stopped being profitable for the arrais (skippers).
items.place: Vila Franca de Xira, Tagus upriver

items.action: Fragatas and varinos survived almost to the present but practically vanished from the Tagus because of ferry-boats and road freight, especially after the Tagus bridge opened.
Thanks to the dedication of enthusiasts and local councils, some botes and canoas still survive as local heritage.
Seixal council restored old local-traffic boats for tourism; they had served between quays and ports of the estuary until the early 1970s.
Botes-de-fragata 'Baía do Seixal' and 'Gaivotas' and varino 'Amoroso' belong to the Seixal Ecomuseum's collection as pleasure craft.
Other riverside municipalities also had surviving boats restored and preserved.
items.place: Moita, Alcochete, Vila Franca de Xira, Azambuja
items.who: municipalities of Moita, Alcochete, Vila Franca de Xira, Azambuja

items.action: Fragatas, varinos and canoas were the best-known Tagus boats; today they survive in oral memory, images, literature, and models in municipal museums.
The fragata, now gone, earned the nickname 'Queen of the Tagus Estuary' for its size, billowing sails, constant crossings between banks and its crew's life at the quay.
The fragata inspired revue theatre scenes and many verses, including fados and songs that evoke nostalgia.
